title: AI researchers speed up 10x in two years, but RSI may be easier than being a paralegal
dek: RSI is a cumulative task — in theory a Python file under a million tokens could train a recursively self-improving model from scratch; but a law firm's paralegal has to remember constantly shifting interpersonal relationships and tacit ways of doing things, which is a non-stationary distribution.
why: The three researchers' disagreements about RSI, continual learning, and RL generalization are very concrete, and the second half's mechanistic explanation of mid-training and signal-to-noise is the most valuable part of this episode.
who: Engineers and researchers focused on the boundaries of AI capability and training mechanisms, especially those who want to understand RL generalization, the continual learning bottleneck, and the role of mid-training.
skip: The opening hypothetical discussion of the 2036 scenario can be fast-forwarded; the mechanistic part starts at 44:38.

points.h: A model seems smart, then a month later it seems dumb
points.body: John Schulman describes a recurring cycle: a new model comes out, people are blown away and say ‘this is AGI’, but after about a month of use it starts to seem dumb again. This cycle may keep repeating, and it's hard to predict how many more times. The mechanism he gives: capability doesn't explode right now because when doing research and engineering you still get stuck on bottlenecks — even if a model can write far more code than a human, it won't give you a 100x productivity boost. Dwarkesh opens by asking: if by 2036 there's no crazy alien superintelligence, what's the most likely technical reason? Beren Millidge's default answer is a Moravec's-paradox-style continuation — AI does extremely well on whatever humans put into a benchmark or environment, but there's always a stubborn sim-to-real gap blocking everything.

points.h: Distillation is the only force against centralization
points.body: John Schulman sees distillation as the main force countering the centralization trend: anything learnable through RL can be easily distilled, because the number of bits is small and a little data suffices. But he stresses distillation is not trivial — when distilling with supervised learning, the prompt distribution matters enormously; you need a real, broad prompt distribution. He mentions something that recently surfaced: some Chinese companies may be running router services that let Chinese users access otherwise-blocked US frontier models, and these services collect and sell data, which is an extremely useful dataset for distillation because it gives a perfect prompt distribution. Charlie O'Neill draws a concrete prediction from this: frontier labs may not have much of an advantage left in RL environments.

points.h: RSI is a cumulative task; being a lawyer is not
points.body: Charlie O'Neill splits tasks into two kinds: cumulative and non-stationary. RSI is cumulative — in theory a Python file under a million tokens could train a recursively self-improving model from scratch, and after discovering attention, mixture of experts, GRPO, you just add them to the training stack without going back to redo everything. The real world is not cumulative: a law firm's paralegal has to remember the constantly shifting relationships among all the important people in the company and all the tacit ways of doing things, which is a non-stationary distribution. Dwarkesh's summary is ‘RSI just happens to be easier than being a paralegal, how unfortunate’. If labs conclude RSI is cumulative, more compute will tilt that way.

points.h: Continual learning is stuck on catastrophic forgetting
points.body: Charlie O'Neill says that at large scale and large batch, the outer loop of feeding data into mid-training does work, but at the micro level — a model doing hundreds of consecutive micro-updates for one law firm — every method collapses: SFT on successful trajectories causes catastrophic forgetting and general capability degrades; on-policy distillation can push that boundary a bit further but will eventually yield. RL is good at injecting capability, not knowledge. Beren Millidge thinks this is mainly a technical problem, not a capacity problem: a model of the same size pretrained from scratch on all the data is simply better; the bottleneck is plasticity and catastrophic forgetting, and there's no good way to stop old data from being forgotten.

Dwarkesh and Princeton's Jerry Han ran a grid experiment: pairing training recipes and datasets from 2019 to now in all combinations, GPT-2 with the latest Ultra-FineWeb, Delphi with an old dataset like Pile, running the full grid. The conclusion is that data brings about 12.0x compute efficiency improvement, while architecture improvements bring only about 3.7x, and at very small scale. Charlie O'Neill says the big chunk of the internet has already been eaten, useful things won't grow at the same rate, and there's probably only a pile of 0.1% loss reductions left. He mentions someone at Epoch estimated 3x per year since 2019, over 2000x cumulative, and the missing 100x probably comes from post-training.

Beren Millidge says this comes back to the RL signal problem: RL is currently bad at exploration, and if the model can't get it in 128 rollouts, there's basically no progress signal, so RL needs curricula, whereas pretraining needs none at all. Charlie O'Neill adds: the pretraining signal is already in Common Crawl, the problem is just filtering noise, which is automatable; but once you get to mid-training and post-training, the signal simply isn't in the raw data, and no amount of filtering will extract it — there isn't a Millennium Prize proof hidden in Common Crawl waiting to be filtered out. You can only get bits from elsewhere: have people write out reasoning traces, construct environments, or use human data from deployment.

points.h: Most of RL's success comes from mid-training
points.body: Beren Millidge says what's underrated is mid-training: pretraining on synthetic reasoning data and environments, warm-starting the model to almost 80% of the way to the final RL checkpoint, with RL just fine-tuning the policy on top. So it doesn't need to learn these behaviors from scratch; a few bits per episode suffice. He also stresses that the signal-to-noise ratio of these bits is far higher than ordinary pretraining — in SFT you have to match another model's reasoning process token by token, which injects too many bits about ‘how it thinks’ and drowns the signal; RL's objective ignores all other bits and keeps only ‘did it get the answer right’.

points.h: One year or three, the difference is long-tail chores
points.body: Asked ‘when can you hire a drop-in remote white-collar worker’, Charlie O'Neill says if it has to operate a browser, probably a few years; if it can send Slack messages and access things programmatically, probably a year. Beren Millidge says full generality maybe three years, but organizations will actively reshape themselves to be more AI-friendly, so you can get 80-90% before then. The substance of the disagreement is the long tail: some chores humans can do will take the model a long time. Charlie gives an example: the model won't ‘yell at people’ to push work forward, it's too nice. John Schulman points out that human remote workers already vary enormously in quality, and on Upwork it's often hard to get someone doing a software project to take feedback seriously; in some cases the pre-AI version is worse than today's AI.

quotes.text: There’s this cycle that keeps repeating where a new model comes out and people are blown away and they’re like, “This is it. This is AGI.” But then they use it a bit, and it starts to feel dumb after a month or so.
We had this very nice straight line and that held for a really, really long time. But there were so many discrete discontinuities and innovations that had to happen to keep that scaling law going.
Basically anything that can be learned through RL can be distilled very easily, because it’s a small number of bits.
It’s so unfortunate that RSI happened to be easier than being a paralegal.
RL is good at getting capabilities in, but it’s not as good at getting knowledge in
There’s no hidden proof of a Millennium Prize problem sitting in Common Crawl that we can just filter until we see it.

An awful lot of what we see as successes of RL actually comes from very, very good mid-training data, which is where we’re essentially doing pre-training but on synthetic reasoning data and the kind of environments that get the model warm-started for RL.

An example of something that it wouldn’t be good at is if I have to yell at someone to get something at work, or really push someone to get something done. The model just isn’t going to do that. It’s going to be too nice.
